newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: North and South Korea squabble over defector's fate.
newsitem.headline: North and South Korea squabble over defector's fate.

text.p: A top North Korean leader, apparently seeking political asylum, was trapped inside a South Korean diplomatic compound in Beijing on Thursday as the rival Koreas squabbled over his fate.
Chinese troops sealed off the building where Hwang Jang-yop, 73, a pillar of Pyongyang's Stalinist establishment, turned up on Wednesday accompanied by an aide.
South Korea lobbied Beijing for his safe passage to Seoul while Pyongyang fought to get him back.
China found itself torn between loyalty to a socialist comrade and a new capitalist friend pouring in investment, and diplomats said it was likely Seoul would prevail.
The two Koreas traded accusations of cloak-and-dagger treachery among the tree-shaded avenues of Beijing's sedate diplomatic district.

Pyongyang said Hwang was a kidnap victim, but Seoul maintained he pulled up outside the consular building in a taxi on Wednesday with the aide, Kim Dok-hong, becoming the most senior North Korean ever to seek asylum in the South.

North Korean diplomats lurked in parked cars outside a cordon of dozens of troops around the building. South Korean embassy officials accused North Koreans of trying to barge into the compound during the night.
South and North Korea were split at the end of World War Two and fought a war from 1950 to 1953, with China battling on the North's side in the conflict.

Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said Hwang was apparently a marked man when he was in Tokyo this month for a conference on "Juche", North Korea's fanatical doctrine of self-reliance that Hwang helped author.
Hashimoto told reporters Hwang's bodyguards may have been tipped off to his escape plans.
"On his departure, North Korean guards were tightly huddled two metres all around Hwang as if they knew he intended to defect," Hashimoto said.

Seoul rejected as "preposterous" any idea that it coerced Hwang, who is ranked 24th in North Korea's power structure by Seoul officials and is one of 11 secretaries on the powerful secretariat of the ruling Workers' Party.
The defection row broke four days before the heralded 55th birthday of Kim, son of the late Great Leader Kim Il-sung, who built a personality cult around the juche creed.

An influential South Korean newspaper published a letter purportedly written by Hwang attacking North Korean leader Kim Jong-il's personality cult and revealing a crisis of faith in the communist system.

"How can a society of people, workers, farmers and intelligentsia dying of hunger be called socialist?" the letter said. "In Soviet-style socialism, the dictatorship went too far but there was no hereditary one-man rule."
"The great general's self-admiration has gone so far that he now really believes he is a genius, requiring the people to respect and obey him only."
The letter added that "every North Korean move is in preparation for war".
The newspaper said the letter was passed to an unidentified South Korean businessman by Hwang's aide last month, apparently to pave the way for his defecion.
Beijing urged calm as South Korea ordered heightened vigilance by its military and Pyongyang warned of unspecified countermeasures against South Korea.
"We are currently investigating and verifying reports about this matter," a Foreign Ministry spokeswoman said.

"We hope the parties concerned can deal with this matter calmly and on the basis of the overall circumstances, and appropriately handle this in the interests of the peace and stability of the Korean peninsula," she said.
Kim Ha-jung, a special adviser to South Korean Foreign Minister Yoo Chong-ha, arrived in Beijing and sat down at once for talks with Chinese officials.

Yoo himself was preparing to fly to Singapore to meet Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen at a gathering of Asian and European leaders. He said Hwang had prepared a memo on his desire to flee the hungry and impoverished North.
